If you're wondering...

Why is diversity so powerful?

A single row of the same plant is the easiest possible target for a pest or disease. Whatever makes one plant susceptible makes all of them susceptible — and once an insect or fungus gets a foothold, it immediately finds the next plant, and the next, without ever hitting a boundary. That's the vulnerability of a monoculture: not that one plant can fail, but that the failure spreads unchecked. Diversity breaks exactly that mechanism. Between any two identical plants stands something different, and that "something different" acts as an obstacle, a detour, sometimes even an opponent for whatever threatens the one species.

The same principle plays out below ground, just invisibly. Different plants have different root systems: some deep and penetrating, others shallow and branching. Together they use the soil at multiple levels at once instead of all fishing in the same layer of nutrients and water. Some roots share nutrients with their neighbors through fungal networks, others fix nitrogen from the air and so enrich the soil for whatever grows there later. One species can't do that. A collection of species can — and the more species, the more of those mutual services arise without you having to orchestrate them.

Above ground, something similar happens with light, wind, and microclimate. A tall plant gives shade to a plant that can't handle full sun. A dense ground cover retains moisture for the plants next to it. A strongly scented plant masks the signal a pest insect uses to find its target. None of these effects is spectacular on its own, but added up across dozens of species standing together in the same bed, they form a web of small advantages that a monoculture simply cannot match, no matter how carefully you tend it.

What all these processes share is that they reinforce themselves once enough different players are present. One flowering plant attracts a handful of pollinators; twenty species blooming one after another sustain a steady population of pollinators and predatory insects that, in turn, benefits other plants in the garden too. So diversity isn't just "more variety for decoration" — it's the condition under which all those individual natural processes start reinforcing each other, instead of each remaining separate, weak, and on its own.

One plant can do little for itself. A hundred different plants, without you seeing it, are constantly doing something for each other.
